archetype.name: Retooling (special teams over substance)
archetype.definition: A team two years removed from 100-point seasons whose power play and penalty kill still work, but whose 5-on-5 play has been below water for a second straight year, leaving it at the bottom of its division.

report.headline: Unlucky at the margins, but the 5-on-5 hole is real and not new
report.take:
Toronto sits last in the Atlantic at 8-14-3, 27th of 32 on the site, and arrives at this week on a nine-game losing streak. The tempting read is that this is a good team in a bad month. Most of the sheet says otherwise. At 5-on-5 the Leafs own 46.1% of the expected goals (26th) and 48% of the shot attempts (23rd). Last season's 32-36-14 team posted a 45.6% xGF share, so this is a continuation, not a collapse. The 2021-22 through 2024-25 clubs that piled up 102 to 115 points are history. The current roster grades out C- at forward, D on the blueline and C- in goal.

What keeps the goal differential from looking worse is special teams. The power play converts 25.7% (6th, more than three points above the league's 22.5%) and the penalty kill runs at 82.1% (8th). That is why the Goal Diff / GP of -0.48 ranks 22nd rather than near the bottom. It is also the reason this team is watchable at all. Strip out the man-advantage minutes and you have one of the league's weakest even-strength teams.

The numbers do hide some bad luck. The skaters are shooting 6.3% in all situations against a league average of 9.8%, the 5-on-5 PDO is 98.2, and Pts vs Goal Diff sits at -5.2, 30th in the league. Toronto has dropped close games it should have split: four of the last five losses were by one goal, including 0-1 to Edmonton and 3-4 in overtime to Los Angeles. Goaltending has been a split story. Anthony Stolarz is roughly average at .902 with a GSAx of -0.2. Sergei Bobrovsky's .874 and -5.0 GSAx account for nearly all of the team's -5.2.

So the record is somewhat worse than the team, but the team isn't good either. The scoring collapse from 4.0 goals a game in October to 2.0 in November is partly shooting luck turning. Some of it will come back. The underlying shot share won't flip on its own, though, and a 62-point pace is closer to the truth than the October .500 start was.

strengths.title: Both special-teams units work
strengths.body: The power play converts 25.7%, sixth in the league and well above the 22.5% league average, and the penalty kill is eighth at 82.1%. The kill has hovered near 82% in several recent seasons, so it looks like a stable trait. Both units are driving most of what offense this team creates. That reliance cuts both ways: it is real, but it doesn't win games when a team is out-chanced at even strength.

strengths.title: Stolarz has held his end
strengths.body: Anthony Stolarz's .902 save percentage and near-zero GSAx over 11 starts are about league-average goaltending. On a team that allows a lot, that is a quiet positive. He ranks 30th on the goalie tab, well ahead of Bobrovsky. Steering more starts his way is the cleanest fix available.

strengths.title: Rielly still drives the blueline
strengths.body: Morgan Rielly has 12 assists and a 9.3 Game Score in 21 games, easily the best output among the listed skaters. On a D-graded defense group he is the one player creating from the back end. His points should hold steady even as the team struggles.

concerns.title: Out-chanced at 5-on-5, again
concerns.body: A 46.1% expected-goals share ranks 26th. It nearly matches last season's 45.6%, which tells you this is the roster's level rather than a slump. The forwards grade C- and the defense D, with Oliver Ekman-Larsson playing 18.5 minutes a night for one point and a 34th-of-36 tab rank. Until the even-strength share moves, the team will keep relying on special teams to stay close.

concerns.title: Bobrovsky has been a drag
concerns.body: Bobrovsky's .874 save percentage and -5.0 GSAx in 14 starts make up almost the whole team GSAx of -5.2. Toronto allows 3.6 goals a game, 28th in the league. Some of that comes from shot quality, but much of it is in his crease. If he keeps getting the bulk of the starts, the goals-against number won't improve much.

concerns.title: November scoring has vanished
concerns.body: After averaging 4.0 goals a game in October, Toronto scored 2.0 a game in November and 2.2 over the last 10. The skaters' 6.3% shooting, against a 9.8% league average, explains a lot of that and should creep back up. The weak shot share means the October scoring was the outlier, not the baseline.

trend.note: A .500 October gave way to a winless November and a nine-game losing streak. The last 10 games went 1-8-1, scoring dried up and the goals against crept higher.

weekAhead.headline: Two hard road games, then two beatable teams
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with three games on the road. Two are against the class of the schedule: the Islanders (9th on the site) and the Bruins (3rd, 15-7-1). Both lean on elite goaltending, at 13.4 and 11.7 GSAx. That is the worst possible matchup for a Toronto team already shooting poorly. Points there would be a bonus.

The back half is where the streak should end. Pittsburgh (7-14-2) has an F-graded defense and the league's lowest all-situations PDO. Philadelphia (9-11-6), at home, is out-chanced even worse than Toronto with a 44% xGF share. Both give up extra points to centers. A split of those two is the floor for a team this desperate. Sweeping them would make the week look respectable.

keyMatchups.title: Leafs power play vs Islanders kill
keyMatchups.body: Toronto's sixth-ranked power play meets the Islanders' fourth-ranked kill and their second-ranked goaltending GSAx. The one edge Toronto has most nights is blunted here. The Islanders' own power play is 29th, though, so the Leafs' kill can keep the game close.

keyMatchups.title: Rielly against Boston's soft spot
keyMatchups.body: Boston holds wingers furthest under expectation of any team in the league, but it allows more than expected to defensemen (25th). Toronto's best route to offense in that game runs through Rielly and the point. That matters more than usual given how little the listed wingers are producing.

keyMatchups.title: Centers feast on PIT and PHI
keyMatchups.body: Philadelphia ranks last in points allowed to centers relative to expectation, and Pittsburgh is 31st. Middle-six centers like Teddy Blueger, with four goals, get a rare favorable draw. Philadelphia also posts a 44% xGF share, so this is a chance for Toronto to win the shot share for once.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal at Pittsburgh and against Philadelphia: Stolarz in both is the clearest signal the staff is chasing wins.

restOfSeason.body:
Some of this will regress in Toronto's favor. Shooting at 6.3% is unlikely to hold over 57 more games. A -5.2 Pts vs Goal Diff is the kind of close-game bad luck that tends to even out. Special teams look like a durable asset. Those three things should lift the points rate from the current 62-point pace. What won't regress is a sub-47% expected-goals share that has now lasted two seasons, a D-graded defense, and Bobrovsky's poor results if he keeps starting. I project a finish in the high 60s to mid 70s in points. That is better than the pace, but well short of the Atlantic's playoff group, which already has five teams at 13 or more wins.

The realistic upside is a team that plays near .500 hockey the rest of the way, with Stolarz carrying most of the load and the power play producing. The downside is that the November scoring is closer to the true level than October was. In that case the pace holds and this becomes a second straight bottom-four finish.
swingFactors: Stolarz vs Bobrovsky split in goal
Whether the 5-on-5 shot share moves off the bottom third

confidence.note: 25 games is enough to trust the shot-share picture, especially since it matches last season. Shooting and close-game results are still noisy.
